keep: Ask what's left standing when the money burns. Buildable assets forgive manias; fixed ones don't.
title: In Defense of Bubbles
claim: Some infrastructure only gets built by people who are collectively, temporarily wrong.
lede: Britain's railway mania destroyed a generation of investors and left Britain with a railway network. Those are the same sentence.
copy: At the peak in 1846, Parliament passed 263 Acts authorising some 9,500 miles of new railway; about a third of it was never built and a great deal of the capital was never seen again. What survived was a network. The dot-com bubble did the same trick with fibre: enormous sums went into laying capacity, an estimated 85 to 95% of it sat dark after the bust, and the next twenty years of internet traffic ran over infrastructure bought at prices no rational investor would have paid.

The argument, made most fully by Byrne Hobart and Tobias Huber, is that bubbles solve a coordination problem. Some investments are large, lumpy and complementary — they only pay if many people build at once — and no individual rational actor will move first. A mania is a mechanism for getting everyone to move at once by making them all wrong in the same direction simultaneously. The capital is destroyed; the asset isn't.

This is not a defence of every bubble, and the distinction that matters is what's left standing. A bubble in an asset that can be built — track, fibre, fabs, datacentres — leaves durable capital and a chastened balance sheet. A bubble in an asset fixed in supply, like urban land, mostly transfers wealth to incumbents and then breaks the banking system that financed it, which is a fair description of 2008.

The historical revision is worth having too. Tulip mania is the canonical bubble, and Anne Goldgar's archival work found the crash's actual economic damage to be small and concentrated among a narrow circle of traders. Most of the ruined-nation detail comes from later moralising pamphlets. The most famous bubble in history is mostly a story about how much we enjoy telling stories about bubbles.

timeline.t: The tulip market breaks. The economic damage is real, narrow, and nothing like the legend.
Railway mania peaks: 263 Acts, 9,500 miles authorised, roughly a third never built.
Post-Telecom Act fibre buildout; the great majority of the capacity sits dark after the crash.
Goldgar's archival study reconstructs what actually happened in 1637 and to whom.
A bubble in fixed-supply assets demonstrates the other kind of outcome.
Hobart and Huber publish 'Boom' and make the coordination argument explicitly.

figures.d: Went to the Dutch archives and found the most famous bubble in history was mostly a literary genre.
Wrote the taxonomy of manias and panics everyone still argues inside of.
Makes the strongest modern case that some bubbles are load-bearing rather than pathological.

facts.s: British railway authorised by 263 Acts in 1846 alone; a third was never built
Estimated share of 1990s-laid fibre still dark after the bust
Tulip crash — far smaller in real economic effect than the legend

contested: Selection bias again: we count the bubbles that left useful infrastructure and quietly forget the ones that left nothing. 'Productive bubble' is far easier to identify afterwards than from inside. And the distribution matters — the people who bear the losses are rarely the ones who capture the surviving asset.
changed: I used to think the lesson was 'bubbles are underrated'. It's narrower: bubbles in buildable, non-rival assets are underrated, and bubbles in fixed-supply assets are exactly as bad as everyone says. Which type you're in is knowable in advance, and it's the only part of the question that's decidable in advance.
